concepts.name: What demography is and why it is studied
concepts.description: The chapter's definition of demography, the three components of demography in Fig. 6.2, how governments and businesses use demographic information, and what the Indian census is and collects.
concepts.idea: Counting people is only the start; what a government actually needs to know is what kind of people they are, because that is what decides which services to build.
concepts.rule: Demography is the study of the composition of human population in terms of different factors like age, sex, occupation and religion, and how they change over time. The human population differs in size, structure and composition -- different age groups such as children, adults or the elderly, different genders, various levels of education, diverse occupations, religion and so on -- and these characteristics change over time because of births, deaths and the movement of people within and across countries. Fig. 6.2 names three components of demography: size; pattern and trend; and structure and composition. The margin defines the structure of population as how a population is made up based on different characteristics such as age, gender and education, and the working-age population as individuals between the ages of 15 and 64 years, who are generally considered the most productive in terms of economic output and participating in the workforce. Governments use demographic information to plan infrastructure such as schools, hospitals, roads and housing, and municipal services like water, energy and waste management: many young children means more schools are needed, a higher proportion of elderly means more healthcare facilities are required, and a higher proportion of young working-age population implies a greater need for gainful employment generation. Businesses assess their potential customers by characteristics like age, gender and income so as to create products that match people's needs. Determining a country's population size and structure therefore helps to better allocate and manage its resources. In India the census is generally conducted every 10 years to assess the total population and its characteristics; it is the official count of people living in a country in a particular period, and it collects from individuals their age, gender, marital status, educational levels, languages spoken, religion, family size, occupation, employment status and income levels. The margin defines a census as the process of collecting, compiling, analysing and disseminating demographic, economic and social information of all persons in a country or a well-defined part of a country at a specific time.
concepts.example: If a place has many young children, more schools are needed; if the proportion of the elderly is higher, more facilities for healthcare are required.

concepts.name: Population at a glance -- how India and the world have grown
concepts.description: The chapter's figures for world and Indian population growth, the bar graph of the most populous countries, the regional distribution of 2025, and why growth was rapid after the 1950s and is now slowing.
concepts.idea: The world's population is still growing, but the growth itself is slowing, and the United Nations expects it to peak and then fall.
concepts.rule: In 2023 India surpassed China to become the world's most populous country, and Indians today constitute around 17 per cent of the world population. Fig. 6.3 gives the most populous countries in 2024 in crores: India 144, China 140, United States 33, Indonesia 28, Pakistan 23, Nigeria 22, Brazil 21, Bangladesh 17, Russia 14 and Mexico 13. World population grew from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 8.2 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050; improved healthcare, which enabled individuals to live longer, largely explains this trajectory. Growth has slowed over time, and according to United Nations projections the population will peak at 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s and then gradually decline as birth rates fall. A projection is an estimate or forecast of a future situation based on a study of present trends, and the United Nations is an intergovernmental organisation. Growth varies across nations: China, Japan and Italy are already seeing shrinking populations, India's population is growing for now, and several African nations such as Nigeria and Ethiopia continue to grow rapidly. Fig. 6.5 traces India's own population in millions: 361 in 1951, 439 in 1961, 548 in 1971, 683 in 1981, 846 in 1991, 1020 in 2001, 1210 in 2011 and 1460 in 2025. The rapid growth in world population from the 1950s onwards came when several medical advancements took place, such as the use of antibiotics, vaccines and oral rehydration solution; better water and sanitation facilities became available to more people; deaths of children due to malaria and diarrhoea came down; and the benefits of economic prosperity were reaching a larger population in several countries. Fig. 6.6 gives the regional distribution of the 8.2 billion people of 2025: Asia 4.8 billion, Africa 1.5 billion, Europe 744.3 million, Northern America 387.5 million, Latin America and the Caribbean 66.78 million, and Australia and Oceania 46.6 million.
concepts.example: World population grew from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 8.2 billion in 2025, but is projected to peak at 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s and then decline.

concepts.name: The four key indicators that determine a country's population
concepts.description: Birth rate, fertility rate, death or mortality rate and migration as Fig. 6.7 defines them, and the replacement level fertility rate of 2.1 that decides whether a population grows or shrinks.
concepts.idea: Four measures -- births, fertility, deaths and migration -- together decide whether a country's population rises or falls, and 2.1 is the line that separates the two.
concepts.rule: The current population of any country is the result of years of gradual change in the number of babies born, the number of deaths, and the movement of people in and out of the country. Fig. 6.7 names four key indicators of demography. The birth rate measures the number of individuals born during a specified period, usually stated as the total number of live human births per 1,000 population in a year. The fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime. The death rate, also known as the mortality rate, is the number of deaths in a population during a year, typically expressed as deaths per 1,000 people. Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, which could be within or outside the country. Birth rate helps us understand how fast a population is growing: if many babies are being born the birth rate is high and the population will grow faster, and if fewer babies are being born the population might grow slowly or even start shrinking over time. A fertility rate of 2.1 means that on average each woman has two children in her lifetime, and it is called the replacement level fertility rate because it is the number of children needed to replace the parents in the population; this rate is crucial to maintain a stable population. If the fertility rate is above 2.1 the population is likely to grow, and if it is below 2.1 the population might shrink over time. Birth and fertility rates are closely linked and together determine the pace of population growth: when fertility rates fall, because women have fewer children, the birth rate also drops, which slows down population growth, and over time, if people keep having fewer children, a country's population might stop growing or even start falling.

questions.q: Two countries both report a birth rate of 15 per 1,000 in the same year, but one has a fertility rate of 1.5 and the other of 2.4. Analyse how this is possible and which country's population is more likely to grow in the long run.
questions.a: Sample: The two measures count different things. The birth rate divides births by the whole population, so it depends on how many women of child-bearing age that population happens to contain. A country with a fertility rate of only 1.5 can still show a birth rate of 15 if it has an unusually large share of young women, while a country at 2.4 can show the same birth rate if its share of young women is small. In the long run the country at 2.4 is the one more likely to keep growing, because it is above the replacement level of 2.1, while the country at 1.5 is below it and its population might shrink once its present large generation of women has passed child-bearing age.

questions.a: Sample: Births and deaths change a country's own population only, and for the world as a whole migration cancels out -- every person who leaves one place arrives in another. That makes migration different in two ways for a planner. First, a government cannot judge its own future from births and deaths alone, because people may simply arrive or leave. Second, migration can change a place's population very fast, while births and deaths work gradually over years, so an area receiving migrants can need schools, housing and water far sooner than its birth rate alone would suggest. A government must therefore track movement in and out of its area, not only its own births and deaths.

questions.q: A minister says, 'our fertility rate has just dropped below 2.1, so our population will start falling from next year'. Judge this statement using page 173.

A population with many young adults already alive will go on producing large numbers of babies for decades even at a below-replacement rate, and the chapter describes the change as gradual: growth first slows, then stops, and only then reverses. Saying the fall begins next year treats a long, slow process as an instant switch, and also treats a likelihood as a certainty.

The 'per what' column is the important one, because the commonest mistake is to read a fertility rate as though it were per 1,000. Migration is given a blank denominator on purpose, so it is clear that it is a movement and not a rate like the other three.

concepts.name: Falling fertility -- population policies and their causes
concepts.description: China's One-Child Policy and its consequences, India's 'Hum do humare do' campaign, the figures the chapter gives for both countries' fertility, and the reasons page 175 gives for fertility falling everywhere.
concepts.idea: Fertility has fallen in country after country, sometimes because governments pushed it down and sometimes because education, work and city life changed what families choose.
concepts.rule: In the 1970s the Chinese government was worried that its fast-growing population would cause shortages of food, jobs and housing, so in 1979 it introduced the One-Child Policy, allowing most families to have only one child; those who broke the rule faced fines or job loss. China's fertility rate dropped from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025. China's population peaked at 1.43 billion in 2022 but has started to shrink, and by 2050 it is projected to fall to 1.31 billion, while the share of elderly, meaning those above 65 years, is expected to rise from 14 per cent in 2023 to 26 per cent in 2050. As more people grow older and retire there are fewer younger workers for farms, factories and offices, which could slow the country's economic growth. The policy also left a whole generation of children without siblings and kinship networks -- an interconnected web of social relationship through blood, marriage and adoption. China ended the policy in 2015 and now allows up to three children, but the fertility rate still remains below replacement level. India made a similar push through government campaigns like 'Hum do humare do' from 1952 onwards, which emphasised not having more than two children; India's population is still growing, but its fertility rate has declined from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025. Many other developed countries -- South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Japan, China, Italy, Spain and France -- are witnessing low fertility rates. Page 175 gives the reasons: improvements in access to quality education, especially among girls; women increasingly getting formal education and working in formal jobs, so they are more likely to marry at a later stage and have fewer children; and rapid urbanisation with a high cost of living, particularly in cities, so people prefer smaller families. Fig. 6.11 sets fertility rate against literacy rate among women for six states: Bihar 3.0 and 55 per cent, Uttar Pradesh 2.4 and 66.1 per cent, Jharkhand 2.3 and 61.7 per cent, Karnataka 1.7 and 73.4 per cent, Punjab 1.6 and 79.4 per cent, and Delhi 1.6 and 83.7 per cent.
concepts.example: China's fertility rate fell from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025, and India's from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025.

India used persuasion: campaigns like 'Hum do humare do', running from 1952 onwards, emphasised not having more than two children but carried no penalty. Both saw fertility fall a long way -- China from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025, India from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025 -- but their positions today differ. questions.q: China's population peaked in 2022 at 1.43 billion, decades after its fertility rate began falling in 1979. Analyse why the peak came so long after the policy.
questions.a: Sample: A fertility rate acts on the next generation, not on the people already alive. When the policy began in 1979 China already had very large generations born under a fertility rate that had been as high as 7.5 in 1963, and those people went on living, working and having their own single children. The population therefore kept rising for over forty years, simply because far more people were being added by survival and by the births of those large generations than were being lost to death. Only when the large generations had aged and the small ones had reached adulthood did deaths begin to outweigh births -- which is why the peak came in 2022 and the decline to a projected 1.31 billion is expected by 2050.
s: Explains that fertility acts on the next generation while the existing population goes on living

questions.q: Fig. 6.11 shows fertility and female literacy moving in opposite directions across six states. Analyse why this table alone cannot prove that educating girls lowers fertility.
questions.a: Sample: The table shows that the two go together in these six states, but going together is not the same as one causing the other. The states differ in many ways besides literacy -- how urban they are, how wealthy, how many women hold formal jobs, at what age people marry -- and page 175 names several of these as causes in their own right. It is quite possible that a third thing, such as a state becoming more urban and prosperous, raises female literacy and lowers fertility at the same time. Six states is also a small number, and Punjab and Delhi already break the neatness of the pattern by sharing a fertility rate of 1.6 at different literacy levels. The table is good evidence for a link and weak evidence for a cause.
s: Distinguishes two things going together from one causing the other
Names other differences between states that could explain both, drawing on page 175

questions.q: 'The One-Child Policy worked -- China's fertility rate fell exactly as intended.' Judge this verdict using everything page 174 reports.
questions.a: Sample: Judged only against its stated aim, it worked: China feared shortages of food, jobs and housing from a fast-growing population, and fertility did fall, from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025. But page 174 reports costs the aim never counted. The share of elderly is expected to rise from 14 per cent in 2023 to 26 per cent in 2050, leaving fewer young workers for farms, factories and offices and threatening to slow economic growth -- the very thing the policy was meant to protect. A whole generation grew up without siblings or kinship networks, and fertility remains below replacement level ten years after the policy ended, so the effect cannot now be reversed at will. A policy that solves one problem by creating a harder one is at best only half successful.
s: Grants that the policy achieved its stated aim, with the fertility figures
Sets out the costs page 174 reports -- ageing, fewer workers, lost kinship networks
Reaches a judgement that weighs the aim against the costs rather than only restating them

questions.q: A state with a fertility rate of 3.0 asks you to suggest a way to bring it down without compulsion. Propose a plan drawn only from page 175, and say how you would know whether it was working.
questions.a: Sample: The plan would rest on the three causes page 175 names, none of which involves force. First, invest in quality schooling for girls and keep them in school longer, since the chapter calls education, especially among girls, the most important factor. Second, open the way to formal jobs for women, since women in formal work are more likely to marry later and have fewer children. Third, support the shift the chapter links to urbanisation by making childcare and housing affordable, so that smaller families are a choice rather than a hardship. To know whether it was working I would track female literacy and the fertility rate together, as Fig. 6.11 does, and expect literacy to rise before fertility falls -- and I would allow years, not months, because the chapter shows these changes work through a whole generation.
s: Proposes measures drawn from the three causes on page 175, with no element of compulsion
Names what would be measured to test the plan, such as female literacy alongside fertility
Recognises that the effect appears only over a long period

concepts.name: Mortality, life expectancy and migration in India
concepts.description: The death or mortality rate and what a low one indicates, India's child mortality and life expectancy figures, what life expectancy does and does not mean, and why people migrate and what migration does to a city.
concepts.idea: Deaths falling and people moving change a population as surely as births do, and both are measured to judge how well a country is doing.
concepts.rule: The death or mortality rate is another important indicator of population growth, and a lower mortality rate indicates the availability of quality healthcare and better nutrition among people in the country. India has made great progress by lowering child mortality from 271 per 1,000 in 1950 to 28 in 2023. Child mortality is the number of deaths of children under 5 years of age per 1,000 live births, and it is a key indicator of child survival and overall child health within a population. Life expectancy at birth in India has risen from just 30 years at independence to 70 years in 2024. Life expectancy is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live if they grow up with the same health, safety and living conditions that people in their country have today; if the life expectancy is 70 years it means most babies born today in that country are expected to live about 70 years, but it does not mean every single person will live to be exactly 70 -- only that on an average an Indian can expect to live up to the age of 70 years. People tend to migrate to other areas for better employment opportunities, education and so on, and sometimes natural disasters and political instability in an area can push people to migrate. Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, within or outside a country, to settle either temporarily or permanently in the new location. Areas witnessing an influx of migrants see a rise in population over time, and cities like Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru have experienced significant population growth due to migration. However, the concentration of a very large population in a limited area can put pressure on resources like water, air and land, and strain services like transportation and housing.
concepts.example: India's child mortality fell from 271 per 1,000 in 1950 to 28 in 2023, and life expectancy at birth rose from 30 years at independence to 70 years in 2024.

questions.q: The THINK ABOUT IT box on page 177 asks what happens to a village when many of its young people migrate to cities. Work out an answer using what this chapter teaches about population.
questions.a: Sample: The village loses people from exactly the working ages, so what is left behind is a population weighted towards children and the elderly. Its total population falls even if its birth rate does not change, because migration moves people out just as surely as deaths do. Fewer young adults means fewer hands for farms and fewer people earning, so the elderly who remain have fewer young people to support them -- the same difficulty the chapter describes for an ageing country. Births in the village are also likely to fall, since the people of child-bearing age are the ones who have gone, and their children will be born in the city instead.
s: States that the village loses people of working age, leaving children and the elderly
Explains the effect on the village's economy or on support for the elderly
Notes that births in the village fall because the people of child-bearing age have left

questions.q: Assertion (A): A falling mortality rate is treated as a sign that a country is doing well. Reason (R): The chapter says a lower mortality rate indicates the availability of quality healthcare and better nutrition among people in the country. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Migration raises the population of one place and lowers it in another, yet the chapter treats it as a problem mainly for the receiving city. Analyse why, and say what the sending village loses.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter focuses on the city because that is where the numbers arrive fastest and in the smallest space: it says the concentration of a very large population in a limited area puts pressure on water, air and land and strains transportation and housing. A village losing the same number of people spreads that loss thinly and creates no queue for anything. But the village's loss is real and of a different kind. It loses people selectively, from the young working ages, so it is left with a weaker workforce, fewer earners and a population tilted towards the very young and the old. The city's problem is one of crowding; the village's is one of composition.
s: Explains the city's problem as crowding in a limited area, using the chapter's list of pressures
Explains that the village loses people selectively, from the working ages
Draws the contrast -- a problem of crowding against a problem of composition

questions.q: Life expectancy in India rose from 30 years at independence to 70 years in 2024. Analyse why this does not mean that people in 1947 rarely reached old age.
questions.a: Sample: Life expectancy is an average taken over everyone born, and in 1947 child mortality was enormous -- the chapter gives 271 deaths per 1,000 before the age of five as late as 1950. When roughly a quarter of children died that young, their very short lives pull the average down far below the age a person who survived childhood could expect to reach. So the figure of 30 describes the average of all lives, not a typical adult life. Old people certainly existed in 1947; what has changed most since then is not how long an adult lives but how many children now survive to become adults at all.
s: Explains that life expectancy is an average over all births, including those that end very early
Uses the child mortality figure of 271 per 1,000 to show how heavily early deaths weighed
Concludes that the change is chiefly in child survival, not in the length of an adult life

questions.q: 'Cities should stop people from migrating in, because migration is what strains their water and housing.' Judge this argument using pages 176 and 177.
questions.a: Sample: The argument correctly identifies the strain. The chapter does say that a very large population concentrated in a limited area puts pressure on water, air and land and strains transportation and housing. But it treats the strain as a consequence to be planned for, not a reason to bar people. Page 176 explains that people migrate for better employment opportunities and education, and sometimes because natural disasters or political instability have pushed them out -- reasons a city cannot simply dismiss. The chapter also points forward to the next chapter for the challenges of urban areas, which suggests the answer lies in how cities are run rather than in who is let in. Blocking migration would also remove the workers a growing city depends on.
s: Grants that the strain the argument names is real and is stated in the chapter
Sets against it the reasons people migrate, including being pushed out by disaster or instability
Reaches a judgement -- the strain is a planning problem rather than a reason to bar migrants

questions.q: Question 10 on page 188 asks you to design a questionnaire for a study of migration in your locality. Draft four questions you would ask, and explain what each one would tell you.
questions.a: Sample: (1) How many years have you lived in this place? -- separates people who were born here from those who have arrived, which is the first thing a migration study needs. (2) Where did you live before, and was it in this state or outside it? -- tells me whether the migration is within the country or outside, the distinction the chapter's definition draws. (3) What made you leave that place, and what brought you here? -- separates reasons that pull people, such as employment and education, from reasons that push them, such as natural disasters and political instability. (4) Do you intend to settle here or to return? -- tells me whether the movement is temporary or permanent, which the chapter's definition also covers. Together the four give me the scale, the direction, the cause and the permanence of migration in my locality.
s: Drafts four questions that genuinely bear on migration
Ties each question to something the chapter's account of migration needs -- origin, reason, or permanence
Explains what the set as a whole would let the researcher conclude

concepts.name: The three stages of demographic transition
concepts.description: How birth and death rates change together as a country develops, the three stages of Fig. 6.12, and where India's own history from 1901 to the present fits into them.
concepts.idea: Countries pass through phases just as people do, and each phase is a different combination of birth rate and death rate.
concepts.rule: Just as individuals experience various phases of life while growing up, such as childhood, adulthood and old age, countries' demographic characteristics also change over time with changes in the birth and death rates of the population. Demographers have observed that populations have gone through transitions influenced by economic development, improved healthcare, education and increased participation of women in decision making in the household. Such demographic transitions are explained through a sequence of three stages, characterised by different combinations of birth and death rates which affect the size of a country's population. In Stage 1 both birth and death rates are high, so population growth is very slow or stagnant; this was true of India from 1901 to 1921, because healthcare was poor and literacy low. In Stage 2 the death rate falls as nations progress economically and better healthcare becomes available, but birth rates stay high, causing rapid population growth; in India, after 1951, the population grew rapidly. In Stage 3 death rates remain low and birth rates start to decline, because of rising urbanisation, higher income, education, and an increase in women participating in the workforce and having fewer children, which slows overall population growth; if fertility drops significantly, leading to even lower births, the population starts to shrink, as seen in many European and East Asian countries like Italy, Japan and South Korea. In India, after the mid-1980s, the fertility rate began declining and is now below replacement level. Fig. 6.12 draws all of this as three curves against time -- birth rate, death rate and population growth.
concepts.example: India was in Stage 1 from 1901 to 1921, moved into rapid growth after 1951, and after the mid-1980s its fertility rate began declining.

questions.q: In Stage 1 of the demographic transition, birth and death rates are both
questions.a: High, so population growth is very slow or stagnant
o: High, so population growth is very slow or stagnant
Low, so population growth is very slow or stagnant
High, so population growth is very rapid
Falling, so the population begins to shrink

questions.q: Page 178 says India was in Stage 1 of the demographic transition during which period?
In Stage ____ of the demographic transition the death rate falls but birth rates stay high, which causes rapid population growth.
Which three countries does page 178 name as places where the population has started to shrink?
questions.a: Italy, Japan and South Korea

questions.q: Why does the death rate fall in Stage 2, according to page 178?
questions.a: Nations progress economically and better healthcare becomes available
o: Nations progress economically and better healthcare becomes available
Families decide to have fewer children
Large numbers of people migrate abroad
The birth rate has already fallen

questions.q: Page 178 gives the reasons why birth rates begin to decline in Stage 3. Which of these is one of them?
questions.a: An increase in women participating in the workforce
o: An increase in women participating in the workforce
A rise in the death rate
A fall in the number of cities
A government ban on large families

questions.q: Explain why population growth is slow in Stage 1 even though the birth rate is high.
questions.a: Because the death rate is just as high. Many babies are born, but many people also die, so the two roughly cancel each other out. The chapter says this makes population growth very slow or stagnant, and it attributes the high death rate in India between 1901 and 1921 to poor healthcare and low literacy.
s: States that the death rate is high as well, so births and deaths roughly cancel
Concludes that growth is therefore very slow or stagnant

questions.q: Consider these statements about the stages on page 178. (I) The fastest population growth happens in Stage 2. (II) In Stage 3 the death rate rises again. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Set out the three stages of demographic transition in order, giving the combination of birth and death rates in each.
questions.a: Stage 1: both birth and death rates are high, so growth is very slow or stagnant. Stage 2: the death rate falls but the birth rate stays high, so the population grows rapidly. Stage 3: the death rate stays low and the birth rate begins to fall, so growth slows, and if fertility drops far enough the population can start to shrink.
s: Describes Stage 1 as high birth rate with high death rate and slow growth
Describes Stage 2 as falling death rate with high birth rate and rapid growth
Describes Stage 3 as low death rate with falling birth rate and slowing or shrinking population

questions.q: A country reports a low death rate and a birth rate that has been falling for twenty years. Which statement about it is NOT correct?
questions.a: Its population growth is speeding up
o: Its population growth is speeding up
It is in Stage 3 of the demographic transition
If fertility drops far enough, its population could begin to shrink

questions.q: A country has just built hospitals across its villages and its death rate has dropped sharply, while families still have five or six children each. Name the stage it is in and say what will happen to its population.
questions.a: It is in Stage 2, where the death rate falls because better healthcare has become available but birth rates stay high. Its population will grow rapidly, because far more people are being born than are dying.
s: Identifies Stage 2 and matches it to a falling death rate with a high birth rate
States that the population will grow rapidly

questions.q: Page 178 says that in India the population grew rapidly after 1951. Which stage does this place India in for that period?
questions.a: Stage 2
o: It was between Stage 1 and Stage 2

questions.q: Using the stages, explain why India's population grew so fast after 1951 even though the country had been almost stagnant thirty years earlier.
questions.a: Between 1901 and 1921 India was in Stage 1, with both birth and death rates high, so births and deaths cancelled out and the population barely moved. After 1951 better healthcare brought the death rate down while the birth rate stayed high, which is Stage 2, and the gap between the two is what made the population grow rapidly.
s: Explains the 1901 to 1921 stagnation as Stage 1, with high births cancelled by high deaths
Explains the post-1951 growth as Stage 2, with deaths falling while births stayed high

questions.q: Page 178 says demographic transitions are influenced by increased participation of women in decision making in the household. Explain how this influences the stages.
questions.a: When women have more say in household decisions, families tend to choose fewer children, so the birth rate falls. That falling birth rate against an already low death rate is exactly what defines Stage 3, so greater participation by women is one of the forces that moves a country out of the rapid growth of Stage 2 and into the slowing growth of Stage 3.
s: Explains that greater say for women tends to lower the birth rate
Links the falling birth rate to the move from Stage 2 into Stage 3

questions.q: Fig. 6.12 draws three curves -- birth rate, death rate and population growth -- against time. Describe how each behaves across the three stages and explain why the population growth curve rises and then falls.
questions.a: Sample: The birth rate curve starts high, stays high through Stage 1 and most of Stage 2, and then falls through Stage 3. The death rate curve also starts high, but it falls earlier, during Stage 2, and then stays low. The population growth curve starts low, rises to a peak and then comes down again. It behaves that way because growth depends on the gap between births and deaths, not on either alone. In Stage 1 the two are close together, so growth is near zero. In Stage 2 deaths have fallen while births have not, so the gap is at its widest and growth peaks. In Stage 3 births fall to meet the low deaths, the gap narrows again, and growth falls back.
s: Describes the birth rate curve -- high, then falling in Stage 3
Describes the death rate curve -- high, then falling earlier, in Stage 2
Explains the growth curve as the gap between the two, widest in Stage 2

questions.q: Assertion (A): Population growth is at its fastest in Stage 2 of the demographic transition. Reason (R): In Stage 2 both the birth rate and the death rate are high, keeping population growth slow. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The chapter compares a country's demographic transition to the phases of a person's life. Analyse where the comparison holds and where it breaks down.
questions.a: Sample: It holds in that both move through a sequence in one direction, each phase having its own character, and neither can skip straight to the end. A child does not become elderly overnight, and a Stage 1 country does not arrive at Stage 3 without passing through the rapid growth of Stage 2. But the comparison breaks down in important ways. A person's phases come simply with the passage of time, while a country's depend on what happens to it -- the chapter names economic development, improved healthcare, education and women's participation in household decisions as the influences. Individuals also always end the same way, whereas a country in Stage 3 may stabilise or may shrink, depending on how far fertility falls. And a country contains people of every age at once, so it is never wholly in one phase the way a person is.
s: Identifies what the comparison captures -- an ordered sequence of phases that cannot be skipped
Identifies that a country's transition depends on conditions, not merely on time passing
Identifies a further limit, such as a country containing all ages at once or having more than one possible ending

questions.q: Page 178 says India entered Stage 2 after 1951 and that its fertility began declining after the mid-1980s, yet India's population is still growing today. Analyse what this shows about how long a transition takes.
questions.a: Sample: It shows that a stage is a description of rates, not of the total. India's birth rate began coming down from the mid-1980s, which is the mark of Stage 3, but the large generations born during the rapid growth of Stage 2 were then children and are now adults having children of their own. Because there are so many of them, even a below-replacement fertility rate still produces more births than there are deaths, so the total keeps rising. The gap between entering Stage 3 and the total actually falling is therefore measured in decades, not years. This is the same lag the chapter shows for China, whose fertility fell from 1979 but whose population did not peak until 2022.
s: Distinguishes a stage, defined by rates, from the total population
Explains the lag through the large generations born in Stage 2 now having children
Draws the general conclusion that the lag runs to decades, or supports it with the China comparison

questions.q: A student concludes that Stage 3 is the best stage for any country to be in. Judge this using pages 178 and what the chapter says about countries already there.
questions.a: Sample: Stage 3 does carry real advantages. Death rates are low, which the chapter treats as a sign of good healthcare and nutrition, and population growth has stopped being rapid, which eases the pressure on resources. But the chapter does not present it as an ending to aim at. It says that if fertility drops significantly the population starts to shrink, as in Italy, Japan and South Korea, and elsewhere the chapter shows what shrinking brings -- an ageing population, fewer young workers to replace those who retire, and pressure on healthcare and pensions. So Stage 3 is better than Stage 2 in some respects and brings problems of its own in others. Calling it simply the best treats a set of trade-offs as a ranking.
s: Names the genuine advantages of Stage 3 -- low death rates, slower growth
Sets against them the shrinking and ageing the chapter attaches to it
Reaches a judgement that treats the stages as trade-offs rather than a ranking

questions.q: Write a short entry for a class display board that explains the three stages to a younger reader without using the word 'rate'. Then explain the choices you made.
questions.a: Sample entry: 'Stage 1 -- many babies are born and many people die young, so the number of people hardly changes. Stage 2 -- doctors and medicines arrive, so far fewer people die, but families are still large. The country fills up fast. Stage 3 -- people still live long, but families become small, so the country stops filling up, and in some places it starts to empty a little.' The choices: I described births as families being large or small and deaths as people dying young or living long, because a younger reader can picture a family but not a figure per 1,000. I kept the order strict, because the whole idea is that the death change comes before the birth change. And I ended with 'starts to empty a little', because the chapter is clear that Stage 3 can lead to a shrinking population, as in Italy, Japan and South Korea.
s: Explains all three stages accurately without using rate language
Preserves the crucial ordering -- deaths fall before births do
Explains the choices made and why they suit a younger reader

concepts.name: India's population composition -- state shares, sex ratio and the population pyramid
concepts.description: What population composition means, how India's people are spread across states in Fig. 6.13, the sex ratio and India's Census figures for it, and how to read a population structure diagram and India's changing shape.
concepts.idea: A population is not one lump: reading it by state, by sex and by age is what shows where a country is going.
concepts.rule: Besides the geographical distribution of population, there are specific characteristics such as age, gender, occupation and education of the overall population that must be studied to understand people better, and these characteristics are known as the structure of the population, or population composition. Fig. 6.13 gives the share of India's population by state in per cent: Uttar Pradesh 16; Maharashtra and Bihar 9 each; West Bengal 8; Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan 6 each; Karnataka and Gujarat 5 each; Andhra Pradesh 4; Odisha, Telangana, Kerala, Jharkhand and Assam 3 each; Punjab, Chhattisgarh and Haryana 2 each; Delhi and Jammu and Kashmir 1 each; and every other state or union territory less than 1. Population composition uses sex ratio as a key demographic indicator: it is the number of females per 1,000 males in the population, it measures gender balance, and it reflects the country's socio-economic and cultural dynamics. As per Census 2001 India's sex ratio stood at 933 females per 1,000 males, and it improved to 943 in 2011, when women comprised 48.5 per cent of the total population; a balanced sex ratio is vital for equitable development, social stability and sustainable population growth. Some states had over 1,000 or near 1,000 -- Kerala, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu. The population structure diagram is a special kind of graph showing the number of people in a country by age groups and gender: the bottom shows young people, the middle shows adults and the top shows elderly people. A wide base means many children are being born, so the country has a young and growing population, like India or Nigeria; a widest middle means most people are working adults, so the population is stable; a wide top means more older people than young adults, so the population is ageing, like Japan. The graph is shaped like a pyramid or triangle when there are more young people at the bottom and fewer older people at the top, though the chapter notes that on paper it looks more like a triangle whose parts have been pulled outwards or shrunk -- a three-dimensional concept represented in two dimensions. In the 1950s India's pyramid looked like a narrow triangle: many children and young people, fewer older people, a high birth rate because families had many children, and a low life expectancy of around 30 to 35 years because healthcare and nutrition were not as good. In recent years it looks less like a triangle and more bell-shaped: the base has become narrower because families have fewer children, the middle has become much wider, showing a large number of people between 15 and 60 years, and the top is slowly widening as people live longer.
concepts.example: India's sex ratio was 933 females per 1,000 males in Census 2001 and improved to 943 in 2011.

questions.q: The sex ratio, as page 180 defines it, is the number of
questions.a: Females per 1,000 males in the population
o: Females per 1,000 males in the population
Males per 1,000 females in the population
Females per 100 males in the population
Females per 1,000 people in the population

questions.q: According to page 180, India's sex ratio in Census 2011 stood at
Characteristics such as age, gender, occupation and education of the overall population are together known as the structure of the population, or population ____.
questions.a: composition

questions.q: Which of these statements about the state shares in Fig. 6.13 is NOT correct?
questions.a: Bihar holds the largest share of any state
o: Bihar holds the largest share of any state
Uttar Pradesh holds the largest share, at 16 per cent
Maharashtra and Bihar each hold 9 per cent

questions.q: On a population structure diagram, a wide base means that
questions.a: Many children are being born, so the country has a young and growing population
o: Many children are being born, so the country has a young and growing population
Most people are working adults, so the population is stable
There are more older people than young adults, so the population is ageing
Men greatly outnumber women in the population

questions.q: Page 180 gives the country whose population structure diagram has a wide top. It is
questions.a: Japan

questions.q: Why does page 181 say that 'population pyramid' is not quite the right name for the diagram?
questions.a: Because on paper the representation looks more like a triangle than a pyramid, and a triangle whose parts have been pulled outwards or shrunk into different shapes at that. The chapter explains that a pyramid is a three-dimensional shape being represented in two dimensions, which is why the name does not fit exactly.
s: States that the drawing is really a triangle, and one that changes shape
Explains that a pyramid is three-dimensional while the drawing is two-dimensional

questions.q: Consider these statements about India's sex ratio on page 180. (I) It improved between Census 2001 and Census 2011. (II) By 2011 it had risen above 1,000. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: A population structure diagram can be wide at the bottom, in the middle or at the top. Say what each shape tells you about the country.
questions.a: A wide base means many children are being born, so the country has a young and growing population, like India or Nigeria. A widest middle means most people are working adults, so the country has a stable population. A wide top means there are more older people than young adults, so the country has an ageing population, like Japan.
s: Explains a wide base as many children and a young, growing population
Explains a wide middle as mostly working adults and a stable population
Explains a wide top as more older people than young adults and an ageing population

questions.q: Using Fig. 6.13, which pair of states each hold 6 per cent of India's population along with Madhya Pradesh?
questions.a: Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan

questions.q: A district records 940 females per 1,000 males. Say what this figure is called and whether it shows a balanced population.
questions.a: It is the district's sex ratio, which page 180 defines as the number of females per 1,000 males. It is not balanced, because a balanced ratio would be close to 1,000; 940 means there are 60 fewer females than males for every thousand males. It is, however, close to India's Census 2011 figure of 943.
s: Names it as the sex ratio and gives the definition
Judges it against 1,000 and says it is not balanced

questions.q: In 2011 women comprised 48.5 per cent of India's total population. Which sex ratio is consistent with that share?
questions.a: 943 females per 1,000 males

questions.q: Using Fig. 6.13, compare Uttar Pradesh with Kerala and say what the comparison means for planning at the national level.
questions.a: Uttar Pradesh holds 16 per cent of India's population and Kerala holds 3 per cent, so Uttar Pradesh has more than five times as many people. Any national programme -- schools, hospitals, employment -- will therefore have to be built on a far larger scale in Uttar Pradesh than in Kerala, and a change in Uttar Pradesh alone can move India's national figures in a way a change in Kerala cannot.
s: Quotes both shares and states the ratio between them
Draws a planning consequence from the difference in scale

questions.q: Page 182 says India's diagram is now more bell-shaped than triangular. Explain what has happened to the base and to the middle, and why.
questions.a: The base has become narrower, because families are having fewer children than before, so fewer people are entering at the youngest ages. The middle has become much wider, because the large generations born earlier have now reached the working ages, giving a great many people between 15 and 60 years. Together the narrow base and wide middle turn the triangle into a bell.
s: Explains the narrower base as families having fewer children
Explains the wider middle as a large number of people in the working ages, between 15 and 60 years

questions.q: Question 11 on page 189 asks you to draw a population pyramid for India from a table of age-group percentages for males and females. Explain how you would build it and what shape you would expect.
questions.a: Sample: I would draw a vertical axis in the middle marked with the age groups from 0 to 4 at the bottom up to 80 and above at the top, and then draw horizontal bars for each group -- males to the left of the axis and females to the right -- with each bar's length set by that group's percentage. Reading the table, the bars for the youngest groups run between eight and nine and a half per cent and then shrink steadily as the ages rise, falling to about one per cent at 80 and above. So the figure would be widest near the bottom and narrow at the top, but the widest bars are in the 15 to 29 groups rather than in the very youngest, which means the shape would be a triangle whose very base has already started to pull in -- the beginning of the bell shape page 182 describes.
s: Describes the construction -- age groups up the middle axis, males one side and females the other, bar length from the percentage
Reads the table correctly, noting that the bars shrink as age rises
Predicts the shape and connects it to the narrowing base described on page 182

questions.q: Assertion (A): India's population structure diagram in the 1950s was bell-shaped, with a wide middle of working-age adults. Reason (R): Around 27 per cent of the Indian population is under the age of 15 years. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Page 181 says India's pyramid in the 1950s was a narrow triangle, and gives two facts about that decade -- a high birth rate and a life expectancy of around 30 to 35 years. Analyse how each fact produced part of that shape.
questions.a: Sample: The high birth rate produced the wide bottom. Families had many children, so each new age group entering at the base was larger than the one before it, which makes the diagram spread out at the bottom. The low life expectancy of around 30 to 35 years produced the narrow top. With healthcare and nutrition as poor as they were, people were dying at every age, so each group thinned sharply as it aged and very few people were left at the oldest ages. A wide bottom and a thin top together are exactly what makes a narrow triangle: the shape is not one fact but the two working from opposite ends.
s: Links the high birth rate to the wide base
Links the low life expectancy to the narrow top
Concludes that the triangle is produced by the two facts acting at opposite ends of the diagram

questions.q: The LET'S EXPLORE box on page 180 points out that India's overall sex ratio was well below 1,000 in both 2001 and 2011, while Kerala, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu were at or above it. Analyse what this tells you about using a single national figure.
questions.a: Sample: A national figure is an average of very different places, so it can hide as much as it shows. India's 933 in 2001 and 943 in 2011 describe the country as a whole, but they describe no particular state: some states sit at or above 1,000 while others must be well below the national figure for the average to come out where it does. Acting on the national number alone would send the same effort everywhere, including to states that do not need it, and would understate how far the worst-placed states are from balance. The chapter itself says the sex ratio reflects a country's socio-economic and cultural dynamics, and those differ from state to state -- which is exactly why it sets the state differences as a question worth asking.
s: Explains that a national figure is an average that can hide wide variation
Infers that if some states are above 1,000, others must be well below the national figure
Draws the consequence for policy or understanding, linking it to the chapter's point about socio-economic and cultural dynamics

questions.q: 'India's sex ratio rose from 933 to 943 between the two censuses, so the problem has been solved.' Judge this claim using page 180.
questions.a: Sample: The direction is right but the conclusion is not. The chapter does record an improvement, from 933 females per 1,000 males in Census 2001 to 943 in 2011, and calls it an improvement itself. But 943 is still well short of 1,000, and women still comprised only 48.5 per cent of the total population in 2011. A rise of 10 over ten years would need several more decades at that pace to reach balance. The chapter also says a balanced sex ratio is vital for equitable development, social stability and sustainable population growth, which sets the target at balance rather than at improvement. So the right verdict is that the problem is easing, not that it has been solved.
s: Grants the improvement and quotes both census figures
Points out that 943 is still well below 1,000, and that women were 48.5 per cent in 2011
Reaches a judgement measured against the chapter's standard of a balanced sex ratio

questions.q: Invent a country and describe its population structure diagram in words, then say what its government should be planning for and why. Use only the shapes page 180 describes.
questions.a: Sample: My country's diagram has a narrow base, a middle that is the widest part by far, and a top that is thin but growing. By page 180 the widest middle means most of its people are working adults, so it has a stable population rather than a growing one. The narrow base tells the government that fewer children are coming, so it should not be building new primary schools; it should be turning that attention to colleges and skill training, since those small groups will reach working age next. The widening top tells it to start preparing healthcare for older people now, before the large middle group reaches that age. Above all it should be creating enough work for the very large middle group, because the chapter says a high share of working-age population means a greater need for gainful employment generation.
s: Describes a coherent diagram using only the base, middle and top shapes the chapter defines
Reads the correct population type from that shape
Derives planning priorities that follow from the shape rather than being asserted

concepts.name: India's demographic dividend and the coming ageing of society
concepts.description: The youth bulge and the demographic dividend, India's age shares and median age, why the window closes after 2050, the pressures an ageing population brings, and how Japan and developing countries are preparing for them.
concepts.idea: A young population is an opportunity rather than a guarantee, and India's opportunity has a closing date.
concepts.rule: A large young population, of 16 to 30 years, is known as the youth bulge, and it is common in countries at Stage 2 of demographic transition. Around 27 per cent of the Indian population is under the age of 15 years and nearly 65 per cent is in the working-age group of 15 to 59 years. Fig. 6.17 gives the median age of population in some countries: India 28, Japan 50, Italy 48, Germany 47, China 40 and the USA 39. India's large working-age population puts it in a uniquely beneficial position: young people can work in factories, offices and farms, or start businesses, and the more people work the larger the volume of economic activities, which helps the country grow. The working-age population also earns money and pays taxes -- a compulsory contribution levied by the government from workers' income and business profits, or added to the cost or price of some goods, services and transactions -- and the government uses that money to build schools, hospitals, roads and parks. This economic growth potential of a nation, resulting from a younger and productive age structure, is known as its demographic dividend. The window of opportunity is limited: the growth in the young population is expected to decrease beyond 2050, the number of children under the age of five peaked in 2007 and has been falling since, and the number of Indians under 15 years of age peaked slightly later, in 2011, and is now also declining; after 2050 India's population would begin to transition towards an older population. These trends have already begun to show in states like Kerala and Tamil Nadu, which are experiencing significant population ageing as compared to Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. An ageing population means more elderly people who need care and fewer young people working to support them: it puts pressure on healthcare systems, leaves fewer workers to replace those who retire, which can slow down the economy, and makes it harder for governments to pay pensions -- a regular payment made by the state to people of or above the official retirement age -- and provide services, because there are fewer young taxpayers. Indian society has had the concept of ashrama dharma, in which life is divided into four phases: brahmacharya, grihastashrama, vanaprasta and sanyasa; though older people begin to withdraw from economic activities, they continue to share knowledge and wisdom with family and society, and cultural continuity becomes possible through their guidance in rituals and storytelling, since they hold knowledge that may not necessarily be in books. Nations need to prepare for the demographic transition. For developed countries the task is to support an ageing society while maintaining productivity and innovation: Japan has raised the retirement age and employed technology and automation to compensate for labour shortages, with large-scale community centres and robots and AI assistants to help care for older adults. For developing countries the challenge is to harness the demographic dividend through investment in good education, skilling and healthcare. At the same time, as more women pursue formal jobs they often face the double burden of managing both job responsibilities and household duties, and a lack of childcare facilities, joint family support and flexible work hours can make it difficult for women to participate in the workforce; supportive family systems and childcare infrastructure like daycare centres can help an economy turn its demographic dividend into lasting progress. Policies in many nations have attempted to revive the fertility rate but have not been very successful so far.

questions.q: The number of Indian children under five peaked in 2007 and the number under 15 peaked in 2011, yet the chapter dates the closing of the demographic window to 2050. Analyse why those dates are so far apart.
questions.a: Sample: The two sets of dates describe different groups moving through the same population. The peaks of 2007 and 2011 are about people entering at the bottom -- once fewer children are being born, the youngest age groups start shrinking straight away. But those children take years to reach the working ages, so the working-age group itself goes on growing for decades afterwards, filled by the large generations born before the peaks. The window stays open while that middle group is still expanding, and it begins to close only when the smaller generations born after 2007 have replaced the larger ones -- which the chapter places around 2050, after which India begins to transition towards an older population.

questions.q: Japan's median age is 50 and India's is 28. Using pages 183 to 186, analyse how differently the two countries must plan, and what each can learn from the other.
questions.a: Sample: India's task is to use a large working-age group while it lasts. The chapter's prescription for a developing country is investment in education, skilling and healthcare, plus childcare and support so that women can join the workforce, and it must all be done before the window closes after 2050. Japan's task is the opposite one: supporting an ageing society while maintaining productivity and innovation, which it has approached by raising the retirement age and using technology, automation, community centres and robot and AI assistants to make up for labour shortages. What India can learn from Japan is that its own turn is coming -- the chapter says India will start ageing after 2050 -- so the systems Japan is building now are the ones India will need. What Japan shows about India is that policies to revive fertility have not been very successful anywhere, so India cannot count on reversing the change when it arrives and must prepare for it instead.
s: Sets out India's task -- education, skilling, healthcare and workforce participation before 2050
Sets out Japan's task and the measures it has taken
Draws a lesson each way, using the chapter's point that fertility-revival policies have not been very successful

questions.q: 'India has a demographic dividend, so its economy is certain to grow fast for the next twenty-five years.' Judge this claim using pages 183 to 186.
questions.a: Sample: The claim reads a possibility as a certainty. The chapter is careful with its wording: the demographic dividend is the economic growth potential resulting from a younger and productive age structure -- potential, not a result. It becomes growth only if the young people actually work, which is why the chapter says a developing country must harness it through investment in good education, skilling and healthcare, and must remove what keeps women out of the workforce. The claim's timing is also loose. The chapter dates the decrease in the young population's growth to beyond 2050 rather than to twenty-five years from now, and it notes that the under-five and under-15 numbers peaked as long ago as 2007 and 2011. The fair verdict is that India has an opportunity with a deadline, not a guarantee.
s: Identifies that the dividend is a potential rather than a certain outcome
Names the conditions the chapter attaches -- education, skilling, healthcare, workforce participation
Corrects or qualifies the timing using the chapter's dates
